concept.name: Discounted cash flow
concept.definition: An intrinsic valuation method that estimates an asset's worth as the present value of its expected future cash flows, discounted at a rate reflecting their risk. Damodaran states the principle directly: assets that generate cash flows have value equal to the sum of those expected cash flows discounted back to today.
concept.intuition: A dollar next year is worth less than a dollar today; DCF simply adds up all future dollars after shrinking each one for time and risk.
concept.mechanics: Forecast free cash flows over an explicit horizon and discount them at the cost of equity (equity valuation) or the weighted average cost of capital (firm valuation), then add a discounted terminal value for all cash flows beyond the horizon. Damodaran's first rule is never to mix and match cash flows and discount rates.
concept.formula: Value = Sum over t=1..n of CF_t / (1+r)^t + TV / (1+r)^n, where CF_t = expected cash flow in year t, r = discount rate, TV = terminal value.
concept.failure_modes: Outputs are hypersensitive to the discount rate and growth assumptions - small input changes can swing value by multiples - and the terminal value commonly supplies most of the total, concentrating fragility at the least forecastable point.
concept.misconceptions: A DCF does not produce 'the' value of a company - it prices a specific set of assumptions - and, as Damodaran notes, many sell-side DCFs are really relative valuations reverse-engineered to a target multiple.
concept.example: Damodaran's lecture example discounts five years of equity cash flows ($50 to $83.5 million) plus a $1,603 million terminal value at a 13.625% cost of equity to reach an equity value near $1 billion.

citations.source: Aswath Damodaran (NYU Stern), Discounted Cash Flow Valuation lecture notes
citations.section: Discounted Cashflow Valuation: Basis for Approach
